notes.definition: Newton's First Law states that if the resultant force acting on an object is zero, a stationary object remains stationary, and a moving object continues to move at the same speed in the same direction (the same velocity).
explanation: Newton's First Law describes what happens when the forces on an object are balanced, so the resultant force is zero. If the object is stationary, it stays stationary. If it is moving, it keeps moving at the same speed and in the same direction: its velocity does not change. A zero resultant force does not mean the object must stop. A moving object only slows down if there is a resultant force acting against its motion.

This explains the motion of vehicles at a steady speed. When a car travels along a straight road at a constant speed, the driving force from the engine is exactly balanced by the resistive forces (air resistance and friction). The resultant force is zero, so the velocity stays the same. If the driver presses harder on the accelerator, the driving force becomes greater than the resistive forces and there is a resultant force forwards, so the car speeds up.

The law also works the other way round: the velocity (speed or direction) of an object will only change if a resultant force is acting on it. Speeding up, slowing down and changing direction all need a resultant force. When a car brakes, the resultant force acts backwards and the car decelerates. When a car goes round a bend at a steady speed, there must be a resultant force (from friction between the tyres and the road) acting towards the centre of the bend to change the direction.

In everyday life it can seem that moving objects naturally stop. A ball rolling across grass slows down, but this is because friction and air resistance provide a resultant force opposing the motion. In deep space, far from any planets, a spacecraft with its engines switched off continues at a constant velocity because there is no resultant force to change its motion.

(Higher) The tendency of objects to continue in their state of rest or of uniform motion is called inertia. All objects have inertia. When a bus brakes suddenly, the passengers tend to continue moving forwards at the same speed because of their inertia: they lurch forwards until a force (from a seat belt, a seat or a handrail) acts on them. Objects with a larger mass have more inertia and are harder to start, stop or turn.
keyFacts: Newton's First Law: if the resultant force on an object is zero, its velocity does not change.
With zero resultant force, a stationary object remains stationary.
With zero resultant force, a moving object continues at the same speed in the same direction.
A vehicle travelling at a steady speed has its driving force balanced by resistive forces.
The velocity of an object only changes if a resultant force acts on it.
A change in velocity can be a change in speed, a change in direction, or both.
Objects do not need a resultant force to keep moving; they need one to change their motion.
(Higher) Inertia is the tendency of objects to continue in their state of rest or of uniform motion.

keyTerms.definition: The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object added together.
Forces whose resultant is zero, so the object's velocity does not change.
The forward force on a vehicle, provided by the engine through the wheels.
Forces that oppose motion, such as friction and air resistance (drag).
Moving at a constant speed in a straight line (constant velocity).
The tendency of an object to continue in its state of rest or of uniform motion.

workedExamples.title: Driving force at a steady speed
workedExamples.question: A lorry travels along a straight, level motorway at a steady 25 m/s. The total resistive force on the lorry is 4500 N. State the driving force and explain your answer.
steps: The lorry moves at a steady speed in a straight line, so its velocity is constant.
By Newton's First Law, the resultant force must be zero.
So the driving force must equal the resistive force: 4500 N forwards.

workedExamples.title: Deciding whether forces are balanced
workedExamples.question: A cyclist pedals with a forward force of 180 N. Air resistance and friction total 150 N. Describe what happens to the cyclist's motion.
steps: The resultant force is not zero, so the velocity must change.
The resultant force acts in the direction of motion, so the cyclist speeds up (accelerates).
workedExamples.answer: Resultant force 30 N forwards, so the cyclist accelerates.

workedExamples.title: A falling object
workedExamples.question: A raindrop of weight 0.0004 N falls at a constant velocity. Calculate the air resistance on the raindrop.
steps: Constant velocity means zero resultant force (Newton's First Law).
So the upward air resistance balances the downward weight.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a moving object needs a resultant force to keep moving.
misconceptions.right: In fact an object with zero resultant force keeps moving at constant velocity. A resultant force is needed to change the velocity, not to maintain it.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that if a car is moving forwards at a steady speed, the driving force must be bigger than the resistive forces.
misconceptions.right: In fact at a steady speed the driving force equals the resistive forces. If the driving force were bigger, the car would accelerate.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that balanced forces mean the object is stationary.
misconceptions.right: In fact balanced forces mean the velocity is constant; the object could be stationary or moving at a steady speed in a straight line.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think an object moving in a circle at a steady speed has balanced forces.
misconceptions.right: In fact its direction keeps changing, so its velocity changes, so there must be a resultant force (towards the centre).

realWorld: Seat belts and airbags are needed because a passenger's body keeps moving forwards when a car stops suddenly.
Spacecraft such as Voyager 1 travel through space for decades without using engines, because almost no resultant force acts on them.
Cruise control in a car adjusts the driving force to match the resistive forces, keeping the resultant force zero and the speed constant.
Loose objects in a car boot slide forwards when braking, which is why heavy luggage should be secured.
higherTier: The tendency of objects to continue in their state of rest or of uniform motion is called inertia. Use the idea of inertia to explain, for example, why passengers lurch forwards when a vehicle brakes suddenly.
examTips: Learn the law precisely: "If the resultant force on an object is zero, a stationary object stays stationary and a moving object continues at the same speed in the same direction."
In steady-speed questions, always state that the driving force equals the resistive force, so the resultant force is zero.
When explaining a change in motion, say there is a resultant force, give its direction, and link it to speeding up, slowing down or changing direction.
(Higher) If a question mentions inertia, define it as the tendency to continue in a state of rest or uniform motion.
summary: Zero resultant force: velocity stays constant.
Stationary objects stay stationary; moving objects keep the same speed and direction.
At a steady speed, driving force = resistive forces.
Velocity only changes (speed or direction) if a resultant force acts.
Changing direction needs a resultant force, even at constant speed.
(Higher) Inertia: the tendency to stay at rest or in uniform motion.

questions.question: Which statement is Newton's First Law?
options: The acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force on it
If the resultant force on an object is zero, its velocity does not change
Every action has an equal and opposite reaction
An object's weight is proportional to its mass
markScheme: 1 mark: B
questions.explanation: A paraphrases the Second Law; C is the Third Law; D describes weight and gravitational field strength.

questions.question: A book rests on a table. The resultant force on it is zero. What happens to the book?
options: It stays at rest
It starts to move slowly
It accelerates downwards
It moves at a constant speed
markScheme: 1 mark: A
questions.explanation: A stationary object with zero resultant force stays stationary.

questions.question: A car travels at a steady speed along a straight, level road. How does the driving force compare with the resistive forces?
options: The driving force is larger
The driving force is smaller
The driving force is equal to the resistive forces
There is no driving force
markScheme: 1 mark: C
questions.explanation: At constant velocity the resultant force is zero, so the forward and backward forces are equal.

questions.question: Which of these situations must involve a resultant force?
options: A train moving at a steady 40 m/s on a straight track
A parachutist falling at a constant speed
A car parked on a level road
A cyclist going round a corner at a steady speed
markScheme: 1 mark: D
questions.explanation: Going round a corner changes the direction, so the velocity changes and a resultant force is needed. In A, B and C the velocity is constant.

questions.question: A spacecraft in deep space, far from any planets or stars, switches off its engines. What happens?
options: It gradually slows down and stops
It continues at a constant velocity
It speeds up
It starts to move in a circle
markScheme: 1 mark: B
questions.explanation: With no resultant force, the spacecraft's velocity does not change. Objects only slow down when a resistive force acts.

questions.question: A boat has a forward thrust of 1200 N and a total resistive force of 900 N. What is its motion?
options: It accelerates forwards
It moves at a constant velocity
It slows down
It stays stationary
markScheme: 1 mark: A
questions.explanation: Resultant force = 1200 − 900 = 300 N forwards. A resultant force in the direction of motion makes the boat speed up.

questions.question: A student says "a ball rolling across a field stops because it runs out of force". Which is the correct explanation?
options: The ball's weight increases as it rolls
Friction and air resistance give a resultant force opposite to its motion
Objects always stop when no force acts on them
The ball's inertia decreases until it reaches zero
markScheme: 1 mark: B
questions.explanation: Moving objects slow down only because a resultant force (here friction and air resistance) acts against the motion.

questions.question: (Higher) What is meant by inertia?
options: The force needed to keep an object moving
The resistive force acting on a moving object
The tendency of an object to continue in its state of rest or uniform motion
The rate at which an object's velocity changes
markScheme: 1 mark: C
questions.explanation: This is the AQA definition. A reflects a misconception; B is friction or drag; D is acceleration.

questions.question: (Higher) A tablecloth is pulled very quickly from under a plate. The plate stays almost where it was. Which idea best explains this?
options: The plate has inertia, so it tends to stay at rest
The plate's weight increases when the cloth moves
There is no friction between the plate and the cloth
The table pushes the plate upwards harder
markScheme: 1 mark: A
questions.explanation: The plate tends to stay at rest. Friction from the cloth acts for only a very short time, so it barely changes the plate's velocity.

questions.question: A hot-air balloon is rising at a constant velocity. Which statement about the forces on it is correct?
options: The upward force is greater than its weight
The upward force is less than its weight
There are no forces acting on it
The upward force is equal to its weight (plus any drag)
markScheme: 1 mark: D
questions.explanation: Constant velocity means zero resultant force, so upward and downward forces balance. An upward resultant force would make it accelerate upwards.

questions.question: A puck slides across smooth ice at 6 m/s. Friction is very small. A student wants to keep it moving at exactly 6 m/s in a straight line. What is needed?
options: A large forward force, much greater than friction
A forward force equal in size to the friction
No force at all, because friction always stops objects
A sideways force at right angles to the motion
markScheme: 1 mark: B
questions.explanation: To keep velocity constant, the resultant force must be zero, so a forward force exactly balancing friction is needed. A larger force would accelerate the puck; a sideways force would change its direction.

questions.question: A van travels at a constant velocity. The total resistive force on it is 3200 N. State the driving force.
markScheme: 1 mark: 3200 N
questions.explanation: Constant velocity means zero resultant force, so driving force = resistive force = 3200 N.

questions.question: A skydiver of weight 750 N falls at a constant speed. State the size of the air resistance acting on her.
markScheme: 1 mark: 750 N
questions.explanation: Constant velocity, so the forces are balanced: air resistance = weight = 750 N.

questions.question: A car's engine provides a driving force of 2800 N. The resistive forces total 2300 N. Calculate the resultant force on the car.
markScheme: 1 mark: 500 N (forwards)
questions.explanation: The forces act in opposite directions, so subtract: 500 N forwards. The car speeds up.

questions.question: A swimmer moves at a steady 1.2 m/s. The water exerts a drag force of 55 N on her. Calculate the forward force she must produce.
markScheme: 1 mark: steady speed so forces balanced
1 mark: 55 N
questions.explanation: Speed is irrelevant: at any constant velocity the forward force equals the resistive force, 55 N.

questions.question: A truck moves at a constant velocity on a level road. The air resistance is 1800 N and the rolling friction is 950 N. The driver then increases the driving force by 400 N. Calculate the new resultant force on the truck.
markScheme: 1 mark: initial driving force = 1800 + 950 = 2750 N
1 mark: new driving force = 3150 N
1 mark: resultant = 3150 − 2750 = 400 N (forwards)
questions.explanation: At first the forces balance (2750 N each way). Increasing the driving force by 400 N makes a 400 N forward resultant force, assuming the resistive forces have not yet changed.

questions.question: State Newton's First Law.
acceptedAnswers: moving object continues at same speed in same direction
markScheme: 1 mark: if the resultant force on an object is zero
1 mark: a stationary object stays stationary and a moving object continues at the same speed and in the same direction
questions.explanation: Both parts are needed for full marks.

questions.question: Name one resistive force that acts on a moving car.
markScheme: 1 mark: air resistance / drag / friction
questions.explanation: Resistive forces oppose motion.

questions.question: State what must act on an object for its velocity to change.
markScheme: 1 mark: a resultant force / unbalanced force
questions.explanation: Newton's First Law: velocity only changes if there is a resultant force.

questions.question: A car travels round a roundabout at a constant speed of 10 m/s. Explain why there must be a resultant force on the car.
acceptedAnswers: resultant force needed to change velocity
markScheme: 1 mark: the direction of motion changes, so the velocity changes
1 mark: a change in velocity requires a resultant force (Newton's First Law)
questions.explanation: Constant speed does not mean constant velocity; a change of direction needs a resultant force.

questions.question: A cyclist stops pedalling on a flat road. Explain why she slows down.
markScheme: 1 mark: friction / air resistance still act (no forward force)
1 mark: so there is a resultant force opposite to the motion, which causes deceleration
questions.explanation: Without the forward force, the resistive forces are unbalanced.

questions.question: A lift is moving upwards at a constant speed. Describe the forces acting on the lift and explain how they are related.
markScheme: 1 mark: weight acts downwards and tension in the cable acts upwards
1 mark: the lift moves at constant velocity
1 mark: so the resultant force is zero and tension = weight
questions.explanation: Moving at a constant velocity upwards needs no resultant force, only balanced forces.

questions.question: (Higher) Use the idea of inertia to explain why passengers in a car need seat belts.
markScheme: 1 mark: in a crash or sudden stop, the car slows down quickly
1 mark: because of inertia, passengers tend to continue moving forwards at the original speed
1 mark: the seat belt provides the force needed to slow them down with the car (stopping them hitting the windscreen)
questions.explanation: Inertia is the tendency to continue in uniform motion; a force is needed to change the passenger's velocity.

questions.question: A shopping trolley is pushed at a constant velocity. State the resultant force on the trolley.
markScheme: 1 mark: zero / 0 N
questions.explanation: Constant velocity means the forces are balanced (Newton's First Law).

questions.question: Describe how the forces on a car change as it starts from rest, speeds up and then travels at a steady speed along a straight road. Use Newton's First Law in your answer.
markScheme: Indicative content:
At rest, the resultant force is zero (for example the brakes are on or no driving force), so it stays at rest
To start moving, the driving force must be larger than the resistive forces, giving a forward resultant force
The car accelerates while there is a forward resultant force
As speed increases, air resistance increases
Eventually driving force = resistive forces; resultant force is zero
The car then travels at a constant velocity (Newton's First Law)
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear sequence with correct force comparisons at each stage linked to Newton's First Law
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct statements about forces or motion
0 marks: no relevant content
questions.explanation: The key link is: resultant force ≠ 0 gives a change in velocity; resultant force = 0 gives constant velocity.

questions.question:
A student says: "If there are no forces on a moving object, it will slow down and stop. To keep moving, it needs a forward force bigger than the backward forces."
Evaluate the student's statement using Newton's First Law.
markScheme: Indicative content:
The statement is incorrect
Newton's First Law: with zero resultant force, a moving object keeps moving at the same speed and direction
Objects on Earth slow down because friction and air resistance act, giving a backward resultant force
To keep moving at constant speed the forward force must EQUAL (not exceed) the backward forces
A forward force bigger than the backward forces would make the object accelerate
Example: a spacecraft in deep space keeps moving with engines off
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): both parts of the statement evaluated correctly with reasoning
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): identifies one error
0 marks: no relevant content
questions.explanation: A common misconception is that motion needs a force; in fact a change of motion needs a resultant force.

questions.question:
A bus carrying standing passengers travels along a straight road. The driver accelerates away from a bus stop, travels at a constant speed, and then brakes suddenly at a junction.
Using Newton's First Law and (Higher) the idea of inertia, explain the forces on the bus and what the standing passengers experience during each stage.
markScheme: Indicative content:
Accelerating: driving force greater than resistive forces; forward resultant force; velocity increases
Passengers tend to stay at rest (inertia), so they seem to fall backwards until the floor/handrail pushes them forwards
Constant speed: driving force = resistive forces; resultant force zero; velocity constant (First Law)
Passengers also move at constant velocity and need no resultant force, so they can stand easily
Braking: braking force gives a large backward resultant force; the bus decelerates
Passengers tend to continue moving forwards at the original speed (inertia), so they lurch forwards
A force from handrails or seats is needed to slow the passengers down
Inertia: tendency of objects to continue in their state of rest or uniform motion
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): all three stages explained with correct force comparisons and inertia applied to passengers
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): at least two stages explained correctly, some reference to inertia or First Law
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about the motion or forces
0 marks: no relevant content
questions.explanation: This links forces on the bus (First Law) with the inertia of passengers (Higher).
